name: Nikhil Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Second-fix carpenter for Delmont Build. They do public jobs, schools, a health centre, that sort of thing, and right now it's a primary school extension on Fenwick Lane. Second fix means the finishing work: doors, frames, skirting, ironmongery, the bits people actually touch. I hang about twelve doors on a good day, and I can tell you the exact weight of a fire door because I've carried hundreds of them up stairs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a door that closes with a nice click and no gap. You fit it, you shut it, done, no arguing. What wears me out is the paperwork they keep adding, the photos of every fire door for some inspector, and the stairs. I've got a smartphone but I use it for calls and the football scores, nothing else, my wife Sanna does anything on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Mostly hype. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, to be honest. Maybe something like, well, there you go, at tea break. I don't post anything online, I wouldn't know where.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, which suits me. I've got eight years to sixty-six, give or take. I'd rather spend them hanging doors than learning some new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up at Delmont, hang my doors, go home. We've got about two and a half months of money saved, and we'd keep slowly adding to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a normal day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the photos for the inspector. Is that the AI side creeping in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, I don't know what's behind it. All I know is I've got to photograph every fire door's label and the gap underneath and send it to the office on an app. The young lad Callum does it for me and I buy him a bacon roll on Fridays. That's my technology plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the next eight years worrying about, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees and the stairs. And whether Delmont keeps winning the council contracts. When the council stops spending, we stop working, it's that simple.

S0.say: Not much, really, maybe a quick ‘well, there you go’ at tea break. I don't post anything online and wouldn't know where to start.
S0.think: Nothing changes, and that suits me fine. I've got about eight years to sixty-six, and I'd rather spend them hanging doors than learning a gadget.
S0.do: Turns up at Delmont as normal and keeps hanging doors. Keeps slowly adding to about two and a half months of savings.
S0.quote: The young lad Callum does it for me and I buy him a bacon roll on Fridays. That's my technology plan.
S0.fieldNote: Few words, dry and practical. He has already outsourced the one digital task he faces to a young colleague in exchange for a bacon roll. His worries are knees and council spending, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of people changing how they work. I can guess who'll be first in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, let's see what it actually does before everyone panics. I'm not against it, I'm not for it. I'd just say wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it probably means more of that phone business, more photos, more checking. I don't think anyone's making a robot that hangs a fire door in a 1970s school with wonky floors, not in a few years anyway. But they might make me prove every door on an app, and that I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much at first. I'd keep my head down, keep the job, and keep Callum sweet. If Delmont made us do a course, I'd go, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not the work, the hassle around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Callum moved on and there was nobody to do the app for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to learn it, wouldn't I. Sanna would sit with me at the kitchen table on a Sunday and I'd get grumpy, and in a month I'd be doing it. I'm slow, I'm not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you say is to blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that anyone's to blame. Firms want to save money, they always have. If it goes badly it's probably everyone a bit, the firms, the government, people like me who didn't bother learning.

S1.say: Let's see what it actually does before everyone panics. I'm not against it and I'm not for it, I'd just wait and see.
S1.think: It probably means more photos and checking on the phone. Nobody's making a robot that hangs a fire door in a wonky 1970s school any time soon, but proving every door on an app, I'd hate that.
S1.do: Keeps his head down at Delmont and leans on his young colleague for the app work. Attends any course the firm makes compulsory but doesn't volunteer.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, about the hassle more than the work.
S1.fieldNote: His unease is about paperwork and digital hassle, not losing the job. He'd learn under pressure, with his wife's help. Notably, he blames no one in particular and even includes himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots doing the hands-on stuff. Hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much in public, I'm not a big talker. At tea break I'd say, well, that's us done then, and try to make a joke of it. Inside I wouldn't be joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty when that hits and my pension's at sixty-six. Two and a half months of savings is nothing. If a robot can hang doors, Delmont will buy one, they'd be daft not to, and I'd be out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the camper van, that's maybe eight thousand. We'd stop the takeaways and the trips to see our son Jonas, and I'd ask about taking my work pension early even if it's smaller. Sanna's still at the garden centre, so we'd have her wage, if they don't automate the tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I don't sleep well as it is. That would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the van, how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rotten. We bought it four years ago for when I retire, to drive up the coast. Selling it before I even retire would feel like giving up the whole point. But a van's no good if we can't pay the electric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the pension early. Would you try anything else first, like other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look, I suppose. There's a few firms round here, but if it's robots for doors then it's robots everywhere. Maybe caretaking at a school, I know my way round those. But at sixty I wouldn't hold my breath.

S2.say: I wouldn't say much in public, I'm not a talker. At tea break I'd say ‘well, that's us done then’ and try to make a joke of it.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with my pension at sixty-six and two and a half months of savings. If a robot can hang doors, Delmont will buy one, and I'd be out.
S2.do: Sells the camper van for about eight thousand and cuts takeaways and visits to his son. Asks about drawing his work pension early, leaning on his wife's garden centre wage, and looks half-heartedly for caretaking work.
S2.feel: Bad, with sleep that's poor already getting worse.
S2.quote: A van's no good if we can't pay the electric.
S2.fieldNote: Quiet in public but privately alarmed, and he jokes to cover it. The camper van stands for the retirement he planned, and selling it would hurt more than the money. He expects his employer to act rationally and doesn't blame them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, not much in public. Maybe I'd say, at least they're giving us a bit of notice. I'd leave the speeches to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, sixty-three is close. Three years short of the full pension instead of six. I could work it, if Delmont kept me, and save a bit more in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put an extra hundred a month away, maybe a bit more. I'd keep the van for now and decide in a couple of years. I'd keep working, keep my head down, and plan to stop at sixty-three with whatever pension I can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a manageable kind. Like a deadline at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. Maybe the phone stuff, if I had to. I'm not going to become a robot engineer at sixty, I'd just be getting in the way of some youngster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the difference between two and five years come down to for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, really. Three more years of wages and three fewer years to stretch on a small pension. Sanna did the sums once on a napkin, and the difference was about the same as the van.

S3.say: Well, at least they're giving us a bit of notice this time. That's about all I'd say out loud, and I'd leave the speeches to other people.
S3.think: Sixty-three is close, three years short of the full pension instead of six. I could work it if Delmont kept me and save a bit more in the meantime.
S3.do: Saves an extra hundred a month or more and holds on to the van for now. Keeps working quietly at Delmont and plans to stop at sixty-three on a reduced pension.
S3.feel: Anxious in a manageable way, like a work deadline.
S3.quote: Sanna did the sums once on a napkin, and the difference was about the same as the van.
S3.fieldNote: For him the difference between scenarios is almost pure arithmetic. He rules out learning anything substantial, seeing himself as in the way. The van keeps coming back as his measure of loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the young ones. I'd probably say it's their world, not mine. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one doesn't touch me, if I'm honest. I'd retire at sixty-six like I planned. Jonas works in insurance, which sounds like a computer job, so I'd worry for him, but he's clever, he'll work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep hanging doors at Delmont, keep the van, retire at sixty-six and drive up the coast. Maybe I'd tell Jonas to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's after my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something short, like, keep an eye on that AI business, son. He'd say, Dad, I know. We're not big on long talks in our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss, picturing a world where robots hang the doors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The click. Nobody would stand there and listen for the click of a door closing just right. Maybe a robot doesn't need to, but I always did.

S4.say: Good luck to the young ones, it's their world now, not mine. That's about all I'd say, and probably only if somebody asked me.
S4.think: This one doesn't touch me, I'd retire at sixty-six like I planned. Jonas works in insurance, which sounds like a computer job, but he's clever and he'll work it out.
S4.do: Changes nothing: keeps hanging doors at Delmont and keeps the van. Retires at sixty-six as planned and has a brief word with his son about AI.
S4.feel: Calm, because it falls after his time.
S4.quote: Nobody would stand there and listen for the click of a door closing just right.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts it past his retirement, so he simply relaxes. His only concern is a brief word to his son. The click of a door is the one thing he'd mourn, which says a lot about pride in craft.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easy. It's the gap: six years with no pension and not enough saved, and I'd lose the van we bought for retirement. What would help is letting people my age take their pension early without it being cut to nothing, if the job's gone through no fault of theirs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you covered it. Maybe that people like me don't make a fuss, so nobody hears from us. Doesn't mean we're not worried.

headlineQuote: People like me don't make a fuss, so nobody hears from us. Doesn't mean we're not worried.
portrait: Nikhil Olsen is a 58-year-old second-fix carpenter at Delmont Build who hangs doors in schools and avoids any technology beyond calls and football scores. He trades bacon rolls for a young colleague's help with the inspection app. Calm when AI fades and uneasy about digital hassle in steady change, he is alarmed by the two-year AGI picture, which would cost him his job at sixty and the camper van he bought for retirement. With five years he does the sums and plans to stop at sixty-three, and with ten years he relaxes completely. He blames no one, and stays quiet in public.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it leaves six years without a pension, too little saved, and the camper van gone.
whatWouldHelp: Letting people his age take their pension early without a big cut when their job disappears through no fault of their own.
